newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Jury out on Axa/UAP merger.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Jury out on Axa/UAP merger.

text.p: French insurer Axa's takeover of giant rival UAP will create the world's second-largest insurer but the jury is still out on its claims that it has pulled off the "deal of the century".

Boosters of the 40 billion franc ($7.55 billion) megamerger announced in mid-November say it is another of the bold strokes that have transformed Axa from a sleepy mutual company into a global powerhouse in a scant two decades.
But others say that normally sure-footed Axa may have concluded the deal too hastily and underestimated the hurdles it faces in absorbing UAP, France's largest insurer.
"Our concern is the balance between expediency and diligence may have been compromised," said Salomon Brothers' insurance analyst Brian Shea, who cut his rating on Axa shares to hold.
It remains to be seen whether "big is beautiful," another said, worried the merger will create an unmanageable behemoth.

The two firms called the stock swap merger a "friendly operation between equals" giving them a global strategic reach neither could achieve singly. But there is no doubt Axa, France's most profitable insurer, will dominate the new company which will have total turnover of more than 300 billion francs.
CONTRASTING COMPANIES
The two companies are studies in contrast.

Axa, the lone French insurer to have avoided France's depressed property market, enjoys a reputation for being the best quality player in the French sector and posted half-year profits up 52 percent to two billion francs.

Its chairman, Claude Bebear, who has steered its growth from relative obscurity, has established Axa as a significant player at home and abroad. In the United States it bought life insurer Equitable Cos and it acquired Australia's National Mutual to gain a springboard for Asian expansion.

By contrast, UAP, privatised two years ago, is seen as stodgy and bureaucratic, a legacy of its state ownership. It invested heavily in real estate and posted a 2.1 billion franc loss in 1995 after taking massive property provisions.
It returned to profit in the first half of 1996 with an 860 million franc profit.

"If anyone can make this acquisition work, Axa can," said Shea. But he said he's not convinced it represents the best use of Axa's capital. In addition: "Axa is inheriting a business mix and set of problems that brings it very firmly back into the frame of mainstream French insurers.
"In the short term at least, the quality of Axa's earnings will suffer," Shea said.

One of the toughest aspects of the deal will be to merge the two group's French networks and there are concerns Axa may have underestimated problems in whipping UAP's domestic insurance operations into shape. "They're not very performing. There's a lot of work to do," said a Paris analyst.
Axa has vowed not to make any mass layoffs but even without layoffs, headcount reduction is a sensitive topic in France, given 12.6 percent unemployment and powerful unions.
OTHER ANALYSTS OPTIMISTIC
However, other analysts have no reservation.

CS First Boston, which has maintained its buy recommendation on Axa, calls the deal "a marriage made in heaven" that will "significantly enhance" Axa's business activities, both strategically and geographically.
While some are sceptical about potential cost savings from the alliance, CS First Boston believes that the deal could yield synergies of 1.9 billion francs annually by 1999.
When talk first surfaced of the match, analysts dismissed it, saying the pair was incompatible because of overlap in their French and British operations and different corporate cultures.

Analysts had expected Axa to grow profits organically after expanding rapidly through acquisitions. Also, Axa had been attractive for its diversification overseas and lack of exposure to France's troubled insurance market. It currently derives 32 percent of premium income from France which afterwards will rise to 42 percent.
But since the merger, many have changed their tune. "Axa has made a pretty good case for the deal," said one analyst.

Fans believe Axa's shareholder-oriented philosophy will be able to squeeze enough value out of UAP to make the deal worthwhile. "Axa will take decisions faster than UAP management which was a bit dinosaur-like," said one Paris analyst.

They also hold up Axa's success in taking over troubled companies such as Equitable in the early 1990s. Equitable, in dire trouble when it was taken over, has become a jewel in Axa's crown and a big money-spinner.

Other positives for Axa include the European network UAP has built up over the past 10 years that includes a sizeable German presence through UAP's Colonia unit, Germany's second largest life insurer.

And Bebear appears sensitive to the need for the new company, which still has to be named, to remain nimble. "You cannot be a strongly performing company in the long term if you are bureaucratic," said Bebear, who will occupy the role of chief executive of the merged group.
STOCK MARKET CAUTIOUS

So far, the stock market's reaction has been wait-and-see. After an initial rise, Axa shares retraced as Axa shareholders sold their shares to buy UAP stock and take advantage of the 40 percent premium for UAP shares under the offer.
Axa's stock was trading at 308.80 francs on Wednesday, down from the 323 francs it reached just after the deal.
Some bulls see the share trading at 380 in 12 months, others are more cautious with a 12-month target of 330 to 340 francs. Some, like Shea, have a 12-month objective of 280 francs.
Analysts say they are waiting for progress reports which Axa says are not likely before late 1996 or early 1997.
"A lot will depend on what we hear on how things are going," said an analyst. "But I have never known Axa do a bad deal." ($1=5.298 French Franc)
